---
title: "evaluation metrics"
---

## confusion matrix

- a classifier's predictions against a binary ground truth fall into four buckets: true positive (tp), false positive (fp), true negative (tn), false negative (fn)

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| | predicted positive | predicted negative |
|---|---|---|
| **actual positive** | tp | fn |
| **actual negative** | fp | tn |

:::

- most threshold-based metrics below are just different ratios of these four counts
- use it as the first diagnostic for any classifier: aggregate metrics can hide which kind of error (fp or fn) is actually accumulating

## accuracy

- $\text{accuracy}=\dfrac{tp+tn}{tp+tn+fp+fn}$, the fraction of all predictions that were correct
- when to use: roughly balanced classes, and fp and fn are similarly costly
- when not to use: imbalanced classes. predicting "healthy" for everyone in a dataset that is 95% healthy gives 95% accuracy while catching zero disease cases
- good result: close to 1, but only meaningful alongside the class balance and at least one of precision/recall

## precision (positive predictive value, ppv)

- $\text{precision}=\text{ppv}=\dfrac{tp}{tp+fp}$, of everything predicted positive, the fraction that actually is — "precision" in ml papers and "ppv" in clinical ones are the same formula
- when to use: false positives are expensive — flagging a healthy patient for an invasive follow-up, marking legitimate email as spam
- good result: close to 1. a low precision means many of the positive calls are false alarms

## recall (sensitivity, true positive rate)

- $\text{recall}=\dfrac{tp}{tp+fn}$, of everything actually positive, the fraction caught
- when to use: false negatives are expensive — missing a cancer diagnosis, letting fraud through
- good result: close to 1. a low recall means real positives are slipping through undetected
- precision and recall trade off against each other as the decision threshold moves; raising the threshold usually raises precision and lowers recall

## specificity (true negative rate)

- $\text{specificity}=\dfrac{tn}{tn+fp}$, of everything actually negative, the fraction correctly called negative
- when to use: alongside recall when both classes matter — e.g. a screening test needs to know it isn't crying wolf on healthy people as well as catching the sick ones
- good result: close to 1, paired with high recall. a test with high recall but low specificity generates many false alarms

## negative predictive value (npv)

- $\text{npv}=\dfrac{tn}{tn+fn}$, of everything predicted negative, the fraction that actually is — the mirror image of precision/ppv, but for the negative class
- when to use: alongside npv's positive-side counterpart whenever a negative result needs to be trustworthy, e.g. ruling a patient out and sending them home without further testing
- good result: close to 1. a low npv means a "negative" result still carries real risk of disease

## why ppv & npv depend on prevalence (and sensitivity/specificity don't)

- sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test alone: they're computed separately within the diseased and healthy populations, so they don't change when the mix of diseased-to-healthy people being tested changes
- ppv and npv are properties of the test *and* the population it's applied to: the same test gives a very different ppv when screening a population where the disease is rare versus one where it's common
- this is a direct application of [bayes' theorem](../foundations/probability-basics.qmd#bayes-theorem): $\text{ppv}=P(\text{disease}\mid\text{positive})=\dfrac{P(\text{positive}\mid\text{disease})\,P(\text{disease})}{P(\text{positive})}$ — the prior $P(\text{disease})$ (prevalence) directly scales the result
- **worked example**: a test with 80% sensitivity and 80% specificity, used in a population with 5% prevalence. out of 1,000 people: 50 have the disease, 950 don't. true positives $=0.8\times50=40$; false positives $=0.2\times950=190$. $\text{ppv}=\dfrac{40}{40+190}\approx0.17$ — only about 17% of positive results are real, even though the test looks "80/80" on paper
- the lower the prevalence, the more false positives pile up relative to true positives at a fixed sensitivity/specificity — this is exactly why population-wide screening for a rare condition needs either a very high-specificity test or a confirmatory second test, and why the same model can look excellent in a disease-enriched research cohort and far less useful in a general screening population

## f1 score

- $\text{f1}=2\cdot\dfrac{\text{precision}\cdot\text{recall}}{\text{precision}+\text{recall}}$, the harmonic mean of precision and recall
- when to use: one number is needed to summarise the precision/recall tradeoff, especially under class imbalance, and both error types matter roughly equally
- good result: close to 1. f1 is low whenever either precision or recall is low, which is the point of using the harmonic mean rather than the arithmetic mean
- use $f_\beta$ with $\beta\neq 1$ to weight recall ($\beta>1$) or precision ($\beta<1$) more heavily when the costs are not equal

## roc curve & auc

- the roc curve plots true positive rate (recall) against false positive rate ($1-\text{specificity}$) as the classification threshold sweeps across all values
- auc (area under the roc curve) is the probability that the model ranks a random positive example above a random negative one
- when to use: comparing classifiers independent of a chosen threshold, and class balance is not extreme
- when not to use: heavily imbalanced data, where auc can look optimistic because it rewards ranking true negatives correctly even when positives are rare; prefer a precision-recall curve there
- good result/graph: a curve that bows up toward the top-left corner, auc close to 1. the diagonal line (auc = 0.5) is random guessing; a curve below the diagonal is worse than random

## precision-recall curve & average precision

- plots precision against recall as the threshold sweeps, instead of tpr against fpr
- when to use: imbalanced classes where the positive class is rare and is the one of interest (fraud, disease detection) — it does not get inflated by a large pool of easy true negatives the way roc/auc can
- good result/graph: a curve that stays high and to the right, hugging the top-right corner; average precision (the area under this curve) close to 1. the baseline to beat is a flat line at the dataset's positive rate, not 0.5

![roc curves plot true/false positive rate and look informative even under imbalance; precision-recall curves plot precision against recall and expose the cost of false positives among a rare positive class more clearly — use roc when classes are roughly balanced, precision-recall when they're not](../../assets/evaluation-metrics/roc-vs-precision-recall.png){fig-alt="side-by-side roc curve and precision-recall curve plotted from the same classifier, with notes on when each is the better choice" width=640}

## log loss (cross-entropy)

- for binary outcomes, $\text{log loss}=-\dfrac{1}{n}\sum_i \big[y_i\log(\hat p_i)+(1-y_i)\log(1-\hat p_i)\big]$, using predicted probabilities $\hat p_i$ rather than hard class labels
- when to use: the predicted probabilities themselves matter (risk scores, downstream decision-making), not just the final class call
- good result: close to 0. log loss punishes confident wrong predictions heavily — predicting $\hat p=0.99$ for a case that turns out negative costs far more than predicting $\hat p=0.6$

## brier score

- $\text{brier}=\dfrac{1}{n}\sum_i(\hat p_i-y_i)^2$, the mean squared error between predicted probability and the actual outcome (0/1)
- when to use: checking calibration of predicted probabilities — whether a predicted 70% risk actually corresponds to the event happening about 70% of the time
- good result: close to 0 (bounded in $[0,1]$); compare against the brier score of just predicting the base rate for everyone as a baseline. decompose into calibration and refinement/resolution components to see whether poor scores come from miscalibration or poor discrimination
- a reliability diagram (predicted probability bucket vs. observed frequency) is the standard graph alongside it: a good model's points sit close to the 45° diagonal

## fixing miscalibration

- a model can discriminate well (high auc — it ranks positives above negatives) while still being miscalibrated (its predicted probabilities don't match observed frequencies) — these are separate properties, and fixing one doesn't automatically fix the other
- **platt scaling**: fits a 1-d logistic regression from the model's raw scores to calibrated probabilities ($\hat p_{\text{calibrated}}=\sigma(a\cdot\text{score}+b)$); simple, works well with limited calibration data, but assumes the miscalibration has a sigmoid shape
- **isotonic regression**: fits an arbitrary monotonic (non-decreasing) mapping from raw scores to calibrated probabilities; more flexible than platt scaling, but needs more data to avoid overfitting the calibration curve itself
- always fit the calibration mapping on a held-out split (or via cross-validation), never on the same data used to fit the model — calibrating on training data just reproduces its overconfidence, see [train/test splits](train-test.qmd)
- recalibration changes predicted probabilities, not the model's ranking of examples — auc is unaffected, but brier score, log loss, and the reliability diagram should improve
- refit or re-check calibration periodically in production: a model calibrated on one population or time period can drift out of calibration even if its discrimination (auc) holds up, see [batch effects & distribution shift over time](feature-engineering.qmd#batch-effects-distribution-shift-over-time)

## regression metrics (for comparison)

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| metric | formula | when to use | good result |
|---|---|---|---|
| mae | $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i\lvert y_i-\hat y_i\rvert$ | errors should be weighted linearly; robust to outliers | close to 0, in the units of $y$ |
| mse / rmse | $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2$ (rmse is its square root) | large errors should be penalised more heavily than small ones | close to 0; rmse is in the units of $y$ |
| $r^2$ | $1-\dfrac{\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2}{\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2}$ | summarising how much variance the model explains vs. predicting the mean | close to 1; 0 means no better than predicting the mean, negative means worse |

:::

## choosing a metric

- start from which error is more costly, not from which metric is most common
- under class imbalance, accuracy and roc/auc can both look better than the model deserves; check precision, recall, and a precision-recall curve
- when probabilities feed a downstream decision, check calibration (brier score, reliability diagram) in addition to discrimination (auc, f1)
- always report a metric alongside the class balance or base rate it was computed against — a metric value means little on its own
